--- title: "[Graph.delete_nodes_ws()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Delete all selected nodes and their incident edges. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L2556-L2657){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.delete_nodes_ws() ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Delete selected nodes](/assets/graphs/delete-nodes-ws.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="Left: a six-node graph with nodes B and E selected in the accent color. Right: B and E are gone along with all five of their incident edges, shown as dashed outlines; only A, C, D, F and the edges A–D and C–F remain." width="100%"} Removes nodes in the current selection from the graph, along with all edges connected to those nodes. Updates selection state and removes the selected nodes from the graph structure. The `_ws` suffix stands for "with selection": rather than taking nodes as arguments, the method acts on whatever nodes are currently selected. This separates *which* nodes to remove (decided by any of the `select_nodes*()` methods, traversals like `trav_out()`, or selection set operations) from the removal itself, which makes condition-based pruning easy, for example: - dropping low-degree or isolated nodes before an analysis - removing nodes whose attributes mark them as noise or out of scope - cutting away a neighborhood reached by a traversal After deletion the removed nodes are no longer part of the node selection (it ends up empty), and their removed edges are no longer part of the edge selection. If no nodes are selected, the call does nothing. The graph is modified in place and, when at least one node is removed, the deletion is recorded as a single step in the step log (see `steps`). To delete just the selected edges while keeping all nodes, use `delete_edges_ws()`. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Self for method chaining. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} Deletion acts on whatever nodes are currently selected, so select the nodes to remove first. Here, the two middle nodes of a five-node path are selected and deleted, leaving three nodes. Because deleting a node also removes its incident edges, only the edge between the first two surviving nodes remains: ::: {#fc919692 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ec.Graph().add_path_graph(5) # path: 1-2-3-4-5 graph.select_nodes_by_id([graph.get_id_from_label("3"), graph.get_id_from_label("4")]) graph.delete_nodes_ws() graph.count_nodes(), graph.count_edges() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (3, 1) ``` ::: ::: The node selection is emptied by the deletion, so calling `delete_nodes_ws()` again without a new selection is a no-op: ::: {#d950f4ff .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph.delete_nodes_ws() graph.get_selected_node_ids(), graph.count_nodes() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` ([], 3) ``` ::: ::: Selection also accepts a predicate, which is convenient for deleting nodes based on their attributes rather than their IDs: ::: {#d2454dbf .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ( ec.Graph() .add_nodes([("A", {"value": 10}), ("B", {"value": 25}), ("C", {"value": 30})]) .add_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "C")]) ) graph.select_nodes(lambda n: n.attributes.get("value", 0) > 20) graph.delete_nodes_ws() # only "A", whose value is 20 or below, survives graph.get_node_df() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ```{=html}
